data.title: Penicillins (penicillin G, amoxicillin, ampicillin, cloxacillin)
data.summary: Other antibacterials · β-lactam antibiotics — natural penicillins, aminopenicillins and penicillinase-resistant penicillins
data.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antibacterials_

**Class:** β-lactam antibiotics — natural penicillins, aminopenicillins and penicillinase-resistant penicillins

## Mechanism of action
- Bind penicillin-binding proteins → block transpeptidation (cross-linking) of the peptidoglycan cell wall → lysis of dividing bacteria (bactericidal)
- Natural penicillin G: streptococci, Treponema, Neisseria (sensitive strains)
- Aminopenicillins (amoxicillin, ampicillin): add some Gram-negatives; destroyed by β-lactamase — clavulanic acid protects them
- Cloxacillin/flucloxacillin: resist staphylococcal penicillinase → anti-staphylococcal (not MRSA)

## Pharmacokinetics
- Amoxicillin is better absorbed than ampicillin and unaffected by food; cloxacillin best on an empty stomach
- Renal excretion (probenecid prolongs levels)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Aqueous crystalline penicillin G: neurosyphilis, ocular and otic syphilis — 18–24 million U/day IV (3–4 MU every 4 h) for 10–14 days
- Procaine penicillin 2.4 MU IM daily + probenecid 500 mg four times daily × 10–14 days: alternative for neurosyphilis
- Benzathine penicillin: see exam-list post
- Amoxicillin (± clavulanate): impetigo/cellulitis (step-down), infected eczema, bites (co-amoxiclav), early Lyme disease in children, actinomycosis
- Cloxacillin/flucloxacillin: staphylococcal impetigo, furunculosis, cellulitis, SSSS (with IV forms)
- Erysipelas/streptococcal cellulitis: penicillin V or amoxicillin

## Dose & formulations
- Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily (co-amoxiclav 625 mg three times daily)
- Cloxacillin 500 mg four times daily, 1 h before food
- Children: amoxicillin 25–45 mg/kg/day; cloxacillin 50–100 mg/kg/day in divided doses

## Adverse effects
- Hypersensitivity: urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis (1–4 per 10,000 courses)
- Ampicillin/amoxicillin maculopapular rash in infectious mononucleosis (EBV) — up to 80–100%, not true allergy
- Serum-sickness-like reaction (amoxicillin, children), AGEP, SJS/TEN, DRESS (rare)
- Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction in syphilis; Hoigné syndrome (procaine penicillin: acute anxiety, hallucinations from procaine embolism)
- Diarrhoea, C. difficile colitis; cholestatic hepatitis (co-amoxiclav, flucloxacillin)

## Contraindications
- Penicillin allergy (immediate type) — avoid; desensitise when penicillin is essential (syphilis in pregnancy, neurosyphilis)
- Amoxicillin in suspected infectious mononucleosis

## Drug interactions
- Probenecid raises levels; allopurinol increases ampicillin rash
- Methotrexate: reduced renal clearance → toxicity
- Warfarin: INR may rise

## Monitoring
- Watch for allergy; LFT on long co-amoxiclav/flucloxacillin courses

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding (old FDA category B).

## Viva points
- Neurosyphilis needs aqueous crystalline penicillin G IV — benzathine does not reach CSF
- Ampicillin rash in EBV infection
- Cloxacillin = penicillinase-resistant, for staph (not MRSA)
- Hoigné syndrome vs anaphylaxis vs Jarisch–Herxheimer

_Sources: Khopkar ch.1 (Penicillins); Wolverton 4e ch.9 (β-lactams). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._
